Newborn Care

Constipation while breastfeeding: relief, laxatives and a safer care plan

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hard stools and painful straining can make recovery after birth harder. Treatment can usually fit alongside breastfeeding, but it should account for your symptoms, delivery recovery, medicines and your baby’s health.

Constipation is more than a count of bowel movements

You may be constipated if stools become hard, dry or difficult to pass, if you strain, or if you go less often than is normal for you. A feeling that the bowel has not emptied can also matter. People have different usual patterns, so missing one daily bowel movement does not automatically mean there is a problem.

Frequency may range from several times a day to several times a week in otherwise healthy people. Describe the change, stool consistency and discomfort rather than judging yourself against someone else’s routine. Breastfeeding does not mean you must leave painful bowel movements untreated.

Why it can happen after birth

Pregnancy-related bowel changes can continue into the recovery period. Pain medicines, iron supplements, less movement, interrupted meals and difficulty finding time for the toilet may contribute. Feeding a baby can also make it harder to notice thirst or eat regularly, but breastfeeding itself does not explain every case.

Stitches, a perineal tear, haemorrhoids or abdominal surgery can make you anxious about opening your bowels. Avoidance may make stool harder and passing it more uncomfortable. Tell your maternity team about pain or fear, especially after a significant tear, so bowel care can fit the injury and repair.

Build up food fibre and maintain fluids

Include fibre-containing foods such as vegetables, fruit, beans, oats and other whole grains. Wheat bran helps some people, but abruptly adding large amounts can increase bloating. Increase fibre gradually and notice how your bowel responds rather than treating the largest possible portion as the goal.

Keep a drink accessible during feeds and throughout the day. Adequate fluids are especially important with a fibre supplement, but forcing excessive water is not a substitute for treating persistent constipation. If you have a medical fluid restriction, get advice before changing intake or starting a bulk-forming product.

Make passing a stool more comfortable

Respond to the urge when you can and try to arrange a few unhurried minutes. A supported sitting position and a small footstool may help some people avoid straining. Do not spend a long time pushing because you feel you must produce a bowel movement on a schedule.

Gentle movement appropriate to your recovery can help support a routine. If discomfort, limited mobility or a baby’s needs make these changes difficult, ask for practical help. Needing a laxative is not a failure to eat well or manage recovery, and a prescribed bowel-care plan should not be delayed while you try every lifestyle measure.

Review pain relief, especially codeine

Opioid pain medicines can slow the bowel. Codeine also needs a separate breastfeeding safety review: NHS specialist guidance advises against its use because the infant’s exposure and response can be unpredictable. Ask a prescriber or pharmacist promptly about an appropriate alternative before taking another dose, rather than simply adding more laxatives.

If a few doses were taken inadvertently, seek advice and watch for unusual infant sleepiness, poor feeding, pallor or slow breathing. Difficulty waking the baby or breathing problems need emergency help. Do not assume these signs are ordinary newborn tiredness.

Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, and anti-inflammatory medicines such as ibuprofen or sometimes diclofenac may be options depending on your health and other medicines. They are not interchangeable for everyone. If you have been using an opioid regularly for a longer period, obtain a supervised change or stopping plan; do not improvise a switch or withdrawal schedule.

Choose a laxative for the problem you actually have

A pharmacist or clinician can consider whether the stool is hard, whether it is already soft but difficult to move, and whether medication, injury or another condition is contributing. Bulk-forming or osmotic treatment is often a starting option, but the best choice is not determined by breastfeeding alone.

Ask for the active ingredient, how to use it, how soon to expect a response and when to seek review. Brand names and combinations vary by country. Products sharing a familiar name may have different ingredients, and bowel-preparation products for procedures should not be treated as ordinary everyday constipation remedies.

Bulk-forming products add water-holding fibre

Ispaghula or psyllium, methylcellulose and other fibre-based products absorb or retain water and increase stool bulk. This can produce a softer stool and encourage the bowel’s normal movement. Familiar examples include some Fybogel, Metamucil or Citrucel products, but check the local formulation rather than choosing by brand alone.

They can take up to about three days to work and need the amount of water specified in the instructions. Bloating, gas or cramping can occur. Too little fluid can worsen the problem. These products are not appropriate for every situation, especially a suspected blockage, and a swallowing problem may require a different formulation.

Osmotic laxatives keep more water in the bowel

Lactulose and macrogol, also called polyethylene glycol or PEG, soften stool by increasing its water content. Some products are sold under names such as MiraLAX or Movicol, with formulation differences between markets. They commonly take a couple of days rather than working immediately, so repeated extra doses can overshoot the intended effect.

Magnesium hydroxide is another osmotic option; LactMed considers it compatible with breastfeeding. That does not make every magnesium salt, dose or product suitable for every parent. Magnesium sulfate is not interchangeable with it, and household or bath preparations should not be used as a laxative. Kidney disease and other health conditions need a product-specific check.

Possible effects include bloating, gas, cramps, nausea or loose stools. If treatment produces substantial diarrhoea or makes you feel dehydrated, seek advice about the dose and ongoing plan. A more watery stool is not always evidence that retained hard stool has fully cleared.

Stool softeners have a different role

Docusate helps water and fat enter stool so it is easier to pass. It appears in some products sold under names such as Colace, but local ingredients and combinations should be checked. It is one possible option when softening matters, rather than a guaranteed solution for every postpartum bowel problem.

Stool softeners do not all act immediately. Follow the particular product’s instructions and the plan given after a tear or surgery. Cramps or diarrhoea can occur. Do not assume every long course inevitably causes an electrolyte disorder; ongoing need and adverse effects should be reviewed in the context of the actual treatment.

Stimulants help the bowel move stool along

Senna, bisacodyl and sodium picosulfate stimulate bowel activity. Many oral products work within roughly six to twelve hours, which is why some are taken in the evening. Timing differs by product and route. A suppository and a tablet containing the same named medicine may act on different schedules.

They can be useful for selected episodes or as part of a prescribed plan. Cramping, nausea and diarrhoea are possible. Some senna products can harmlessly alter urine colour, but unexpected bleeding or concerning urine changes still need assessment. Use standardised products rather than an uncertain herbal cleanse.

Repeated unsupervised dose increases are unwise, but using a stimulant does not prove that the bowel has become permanently unable to work. Some people need longer treatment under supervision. Discuss persistent need instead of suddenly abandoning prescribed care out of fear of dependence.

Suppositories and enemas act locally

Rectal treatments include glycerol, also called glycerin, or bisacodyl suppositories and selected enemas. Their mechanisms differ: some soften or lubricate stool locally, while others stimulate evacuation. They should not all be described as identical products that empty the entire bowel.

They can cause rectal irritation, cramps or diarrhoea. Ask before using one if you have significant anal pain, bleeding, a recent repair or another rectal condition. Do not insert repeated products or try to remove stool yourself when there may be impaction or an injury. An adult product is not a treatment to pass on to the baby.

What breastfeeding compatibility means

Many commonly used laxatives have little systemic absorption, so exposure through milk is low. NHS specialist guidance supports commonly used fibre, osmotic, stimulant and local options for parents feeding a healthy full-term infant. The choice still needs to fit the parent’s condition and the exact medicine.

Tell the pharmacist if your baby was premature, is unwell or takes medicines, and mention all your own treatments. For certain products, precautionary observation for infant diarrhoea, vomiting, irritability or feeding changes may be advised. These effects are not expected with every laxative, and a change in a breastfed baby’s normally loose stool does not automatically show a drug reaction.

Persistent watery stools, reduced feeding or fewer wet nappies in the baby deserve advice. Do not stop breastfeeding automatically because you need constipation treatment. A prescription medicine for refractory constipation, such as prucalopride, needs its own assessment rather than being grouped with routine first choices.

Avoid excessive use and recognise adverse effects

Taking more than directed or combining products without a plan can cause diarrhoea, dehydration and electrolyte disturbances. Symptoms may include unusual weakness, dizziness or feeling unwell. The risk depends on the preparation, dose, duration and medical history, rather than applying equally to every occasional laxative dose.

Read the leaflet, use the agreed amount and allow the expected response time. Do not use laxatives as a weight-loss or cleansing method. If you repeatedly need more treatment, the next step is reassessment of the cause and regimen, not an endless cycle of stronger doses.

Check interactions and medical conditions

Bring a full list of prescriptions, over-the-counter products and supplements. Some laxatives can affect how other medicines are absorbed or need to be taken at a different time. Certain antibiotics and medicines used for heart or bone conditions are examples that may need a pharmacist’s check; the interaction depends on the ingredients.

Kidney disease, heart conditions, dehydration, swallowing difficulties and suspected bowel obstruction can change the choice. Severe unexplained abdominal pain should not be treated by assuming constipation is the only possibility. If a clinician suspects an obstruction or another acute abdominal illness, adding a laxative may be inappropriate.

Pregnancy and childhood need separate advice

If you are pregnant again while breastfeeding, tell the prescriber. Several laxatives can be used in pregnancy when recommended, but the choice should consider both situations. Stimulants are not automatically proven harmful to the fetus; they are often considered after other approaches have not helped.

Do not apply an adult dose or product plan to a child. Children, including babies, need age-appropriate advice, and the cause of constipation can differ. A laxative suitable for the breastfeeding parent does not establish that it is suitable to give directly to the infant.

Agree on duration and a stopping plan

For constipation treated with a shop-bought medicine, follow its short-term instructions and seek advice if it does not help within the stated time or if you still need it after about a week. You do not have to wait a week if symptoms are worsening or a warning sign appears.

Longer prescribed use is different from prolonged unsupervised use. Ask when the bowel pattern should be reviewed and whether the medicine should be reduced gradually as things improve. Do not conclude that needing a medicine means your bowel is damaged, but do not let persistent symptoms go unexplained either.

Know when to seek urgent help

Severe or worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, a markedly swollen abdomen or inability to pass gas needs prompt medical assessment, particularly after surgery. Substantial rectal bleeding, black stool, collapse or faintness with bleeding also needs urgent care. Do not respond by taking another laxative and waiting for it to work.

Arrange a clinical review for blood in the stool, recurring constipation, a new unexplained bowel-pattern change, persistent fatigue or symptoms that do not improve with treatment. Haemorrhoids are one possible source of bleeding after birth, but they should not be assumed to explain every episode.

Bring useful details to the follow-up

Note the last comfortable bowel movement, stool consistency, pain, bleeding and what you have tried, including the exact product and duration. Mention recent delivery injuries, surgery, iron or pain medicines, and your baby’s age and health. These details make it easier to adjust a plan without repeating unsuccessful treatment.

The aim is a comfortable, sustainable bowel pattern that supports recovery and feeding. Food, fluids, movement, pain control and medicine can work together. If constipation continues, ask what further assessment is needed rather than accepting either endless self-treatment or unnecessary suffering as part of new parenthood.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Choose a laxative according to the clinical problem and exact ingredient. Many common options are compatible with breastfeeding a healthy full-term infant.

Codeine needs prompt review during breastfeeding. Ongoing constipation, adverse effects or warning symptoms need a care plan rather than repeated unsupervised dose increases.

How BeMama can help

Keep the product name and a short record of symptoms so a pharmacist or clinician can help you adjust treatment without disrupting feeding unnecessarily.

When to seek help

Clinical and pharmacy review remain pending. Severe abdominal symptoms, significant bleeding or infant breathing problems require urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Constipation includes difficult or hard stools, not simply missing a daily bowel movement.
  • Bulk-forming, osmotic, softening, stimulant and rectal treatments work differently.
  • Breastfeeding compatibility does not remove the need to check other medicines and health conditions.
  • Longer prescribed treatment is different from uncontrolled overuse; agree on follow-up.

Frequently asked questions

Must I pass a stool every day?

No. Usual frequency varies. A change from your normal pattern, hard stool, straining and discomfort are more useful clues than a daily target.

Do I need to stop breastfeeding to take a laxative?

Usually not for commonly used products, but check the exact medicine and tell the pharmacist if your baby is premature or unwell.

Which laxative works fastest?

It depends on the ingredient and route. Fibre and many osmotic products take days; oral stimulants often act overnight, and rectal products have their own timing. Faster is not necessarily more appropriate.

Is a familiar brand enough to identify the medicine?

No. Ingredients and combinations can vary between products and countries. Check the active ingredient and formulation, especially with bowel-preparation or combination products.

Can I take codeine and simply add more fibre?

Codeine requires a breastfeeding safety review as well as constipation care. Contact a pharmacist or prescriber promptly about an alternative. Infant unusual sleepiness, poor feeding or breathing changes need urgent attention.

Does needing a stimulant mean my bowel is permanently damaged?

No. Persistent need deserves review, but it is not proof of permanent damage. Some people need supervised longer treatment; avoid unsupervised dose increases or stopping a prescribed plan out of fear.

Can laxatives affect my baby’s stools?

For many common products significant exposure through milk is unlikely. Some advice includes watching for diarrhoea or irritability as a precaution. Persistent watery stools or poor feeding should be discussed rather than assumed to be a drug effect.

Can I use magnesium bath salts for constipation?

No. Do not substitute household or bath preparations for a labelled medicine. Magnesium products are not interchangeable and may be unsuitable with certain medical conditions.

Should I wait seven days if I develop severe pain or vomiting?

No. Severe or worsening pain, repeated vomiting, marked abdominal swelling, inability to pass gas or substantial bleeding needs prompt assessment, not another home-treatment trial.

Can I give my baby the same laxative?

Not on the basis that it is suitable for you. Babies and children need their own assessment, ingredient and dose advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
